This tutorial is intended to assist the user in getting started with calculating centroids of discrete probability distributions relative to the Jeffreys and Jensen-Shannon divergences with the package `{igcentroids}` and integrating these computation in a clustering-task workflow. 
It starts with a short, technical presentation of the underlying S3 classes of R objects the package is built upon, in @sec-vig_catdist_presclasses. The informational geometric theoretical foundation of the ensueing procedures is outlined in Setions [-@sec-vig_catdist_presdivergences] and [-@sec-vig_catdist_prescentroids]. More precisely, the definitions and properties of Kullback-Leibler (KL), Jeffreys (J) and Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergences (div) and related centroids are reviewed; the usage of methods for computing them is also illustrated. 
These procedures fully integrate into a clustering-task workflow performed with the package `{flexclust}`, as illustrated in @sec-vig_catdist_clustering. Finally, full examples of such clustering tasks are presented in @sec-vig_catdist_fullexamples.

As a preliminary step, load the package `{igcentroids}`, as follows.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(igcentroids)
```

It is implicitly assumed that the package `{igcentroids}` has been previously installed; if not, please, refer to the [README](https://github.com/pregnault/igcentroids) file on top of the repository of the package.


## S3 classes `igccatdist`, `igccatdistn`, `igcmatcatdist` and `igcmatcatdistn` {#ssec-vig_catdist_presclasses}

`{igcentroids}` provides several procedures for clustering categorical -- or finite-state space -- (probability) distributions with same support. 

We formally denote $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ the set of positive measures -- or categorical distributions -- on the finite set $\mathcal{X} = \{x_1, \cdots, x_d\}$. Such a measure $\mu$ is mathematically identifiable to the vector $(\mu(x_1), \cdots, \mu(x_d)) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with  $\mu(x_i) >0$  for all $i \i \{1, \cdots, d\}$; it is represented in `{igcentroids}` as an object of S3 class `igccatdist` built upon classical numeric vectors. Such an object is obtained as the output of the eponyme constructor function `igccatdist()`, taking a positive numeric vector as input.

```{r}
#| label: creating_igccatdist_object
set.seed(679)
# A positive measure on a 5-state space
p <- igccatdist(sample(1:10, size = 5L, replace = TRUE))
```

`igccatdist` objects are positive numeric vectors with two attributes `class` and `mass`. The first one is obviously `"igccatdist"` while the second is the mass of the whole set of states i.e., the sum of the components of the vector. Both attributes are displayed when the object is printed.

```{r}
#| label: printing_igccatdist_object
print(p)
```

Note that a validation function prevents the user to convert into `igccatdist` non-positive vectors.

```{r}
#| label: error_non-positive_entries_igccatdist
#| error: true 
igccatdist(c(1, 0))
igccatdist(-(1:3))
```

The subset $\mathcal{P}_1(\mathcal{X}) \subset \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ of positive measures with mass equal to one is of foundamental interest in any field related to probability theory. Its elements are probability measures, called here normalized categorical distributions; they are represented in `{igcentroids}` as objects of class `igccatdistn`, unformally inheriting from `igccatdist`. 

```{r}
#| label: creating_igccatdistn_object
# The binomial distribution of parameters n = 4 and p = 0.5 as an igccatdist object
q <- igccatdistn(dbinom(x = 0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.5))
print(q)
# Normalize a positive vector prior to convert it to igccatdistn
p <- undo_igc(p) # Remove class igccatdist to retrieve a numeric vector
igccatdistn(p/sum(p))
```

Sets of (normalized) categorical distributions on the same support are represented as positive matrices -- stochastic matrices for normalized categorical distributions; dedicated classes are introduced in `{igcentroids}` : `igcmatcatdist` and `igcmatcatdistn`.

```{r}
#| label: creating_igcmatcatdist
matcd <- matrix(c(p, q), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
igcmatcatdist(matcd)
matncd <- matrix(c(p/sum(p), q), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
igcmatcatdistn(matncd)
```

Methods for generics plot() and points() associated to `igccatdistn` and `igcmatcatdistn` are available. Their behaviour depends on the size $|\mathcal{X}|$ of the support $\mathcal{X}$. More precisely, Two-state and three-state supports benefit of particular representations, for mere of pedagogical purpose, as illustrated by Figures [-@fig-23statencdplot-1] and [-@fig-23statencdplot-2].

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| label: fig-23statencdplot
#| fig-cap: Examples of representations of normalized categorical distributions obtained with the methods `plot()` and `points()` for `igcmatcatdistn` objects.
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - Two-state ncds are represented as points on a unite segment.
#|   - Three-state ncds are represented as points in the 2D simplex identified to the equilateral triangle.
# Two-state  categorical distributions plot
u <- c(0.5, 0.5)
p1 <- c(0.3, 0.7)
p2 <- c(0.4, 0.6)
x <- igcmatcatdistn(matrix(c(u, p1, p2),
                     nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE))
plot(x)
# Three-state categorical distributions plot
runifsimplex <- function(n = 1L) {
  x <- runif(n)
  y <- runif(n, min = 0, max = 1-x)
  res <- igcmatcatdistn(matrix(c(x,y, 1-x-y), ncol = 3, byrow = FALSE))
  return(res)
}
set.seed(527)
sampsimp <- runifsimplex(n = 32L)
plot(sampsimp)
```

Nprmalized categorical distributions with bigger state spaces are represented as polylines i.e., continuous piecewise linear functions linking the top of bars in a classical barplot; see @fig-plotbigstatespacencd.

```{r}
#| label: fig-plotbigstatespacencd
#| fig-cap: To be continued
p <- sample(1:10, size = 10L, replace = TRUE)
p <- igccatdistn(p/sum(p))
plot(p)
```
